title: The boy who never heard "no cakes"
hookLine: a commentary story: Anuruddha was so rich he didn't know the words "there isn't"; grown up, he learns from his brother that the farm work never ends (Vinaya, Cullavagga 7)
tomorrow: Eight thoughts of a great person

cards: A golden bowl, with a lid on it, carried from a mother to her son. The boy is Anuruddha, a Sakyan remembered as a cousin of the Buddha, and the commentaries tell this story about his childhood.
He's playing a game with friends, and the stakes are cakes. He loses, and sends a servant home to his mother: send cakes. She does.
He loses again, and again. Finally his mother sends word back: there are no cakes. Anuruddha, the story says, has never heard the words there isn't.
He assumes it's a new kind of cake, and sends back: then send me some no-cakes.

teach.b: In the commentary, his mother decides to teach him what there isn't means, and sends an empty bowl with the lid on.

It says devas filled the bowl with heavenly cakes on the way, because of a gift Anuruddha had made in an earlier life. So the boy who had never heard no still doesn't hear it. Second, years later, in the Vinaya.

His older brother, Mahanama, says someone from their family ought to go forth, and it should be one of them. Anuruddha says he's too delicate for that life. So Mahanama explains what staying home involves.
The fields must be plowed, then sown, watered, drained, weeded, reaped, gathered, threshed.
Third, Anuruddha's question: when does the work end? It doesn't, his brother says. Our father and grandfather died with the work still going.
Now Anuruddha hears what was underneath every cake: a household's work that never ends. Then you look after the house, he says. I'll go forth.
Fourth, here's one way to read the two stories together.
Comfort can be exactly this: never hearing there isn't, because someone else hears it for you.
His mother heard it. His brother would go on hearing it in the fields. The story doesn't mock the boy.
It shows the moment he finally asks where things come from, and the answer turns him toward going forth.

how: Teachers in Theravada communities tell Anuruddha's childhood story with a smile, and the Vinaya's farm conversation is read as a picture of the household work that monastics leave behind and that lay supporters still carry.

o: the endless work of plowing a field
a cake given as a prize in a game
there is not; the words he'd never heard

games.q: Anuruddha's cakes and fields: tap the pairs.
p: explains the work of the fields

s: in the commentary story, the bowl arrives empty
the story says devas filled it with heavenly cakes, because of a gift he made in an earlier life.
the conversation about plowing and threshing is in the Vinaya itself
Cullavagga 7 tells how Mahanama explains the household work, and Anuruddha chooses to go forth.
Anuruddha grew up poor and never had cakes
he was a Sakyan, so well provided for that, in the story, he had never heard "there isn't".

games.q: you're Anuruddha, a small boy. you've lost the game again, and your mother sends word: there are no cakes. what do you do?
games.why: he has never heard "there isn't", so he assumes no-cakes are a new kind of cake, and asks for some.

practice: Find one thing in your day that came to you without you ever hearing there isn't: hot water, a quiet room, food in the cupboard, a language people understand when you speak.
Follow it back, the way Mahanama walked his brother through the fields, and ask who carried it here, who heard no so you didn't have to. No guilt is needed; just see them, for a few breaths.

wordCard.voice: Natthi, there is not. The words Anuruddha had never heard, until his brother showed him the farm work that never ends. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali natthi: there is not. In the commentary story, the word the boy had never heard.

carryVoice: Your line: there isn't. Someone, somewhere, hears the no for you. Day seven hundred forty-eight, done.

sources.ref: Pali commentaries on Anuruddha (the 'no cakes' story; e.g. Manorathapurani on AN 1, and the Dhammapada and Theragatha commentaries)
